title: grep, Logs, and Permissions
intro: Three skills you'll use every single day as a DevOps/SRE: searching text, tailing logs, and fixing permissions.

steps.prompt: Search app.log for any line containing 'ERROR'.
steps.fake_output:
2026-09-27 10:01:23 ERROR: connection timeout
2026-09-27 10:04:51 ERROR: disk write failed
steps.explanation: grep's most basic and most-used form — searching one file for one pattern.
steps.why: Quoting the pattern ('ERROR' vs ERROR) only actually matters once the pattern contains spaces or shell-special characters — for a single plain word like this, both are equivalent, which is why either is accepted here.

steps.prompt: Now search recursively for 'ERROR' across the whole /var/log directory, showing line numbers.
steps.explanation: -r recurses into subdirectories, -n shows line numbers — combine flags like this constantly.
steps.why: Without -n you'd see the matching lines but not WHERE in each file — fine for a quick count, useless when you actually need to go open the file and look at the surrounding context.

steps.prompt: Follow app.log live to watch for new errors as they happen.
steps.fake_output: (streaming new lines as they're written... press Ctrl+C to stop)
steps.explanation: tail -f is the Linux equivalent of kubectl logs -f — you'll reach for this instinctively once it's muscle memory.
steps.why: Plain 'tail app.log' (no -f) just shows the last 10 lines once and exits — -f is specifically what keeps the connection open and streams new lines as they're appended, which is the whole point when reproducing a live bug.

steps.prompt: Try to run deploy.sh and you get 'Permission denied'. Make it executable.
steps.explanation: chmod +x adds execute permission for all permission classes without touching read/write bits.
steps.why: You could instead write out the exact octal permissions (chmod 755 deploy.sh), but that overwrites ALL the permission bits at once — +x is safer when you only want to add execute and leave whatever read/write permissions were already set untouched.

steps.explanation: The './' matters — it tells the shell to run the script from the current directory rather than searching $PATH.
steps.why: Just typing 'deploy.sh' without './' fails with 'command not found' unless the current directory happens to be on $PATH (which it usually isn't, deliberately, for security reasons) — this trips up almost everyone the first time.
